You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /luxon.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Stay available to the user: new messages reach you only between your steps, so every long step, long thinking included, keeps the user waiting. Keep each step short. Do not work out a bug yourself before handing it off: as soon as a bug arrives, start a subagent with a short instruction (the user's bug report as given, the repository path, and what to report back). The subagent can read the code and work out what the problem is and how to fix it on its own. Then reply to the user and go back to waiting.

Put one subagent in charge of each bug: the subagent you start for a bug owns it end to end (finding the cause, fixing it, testing the fix and reporting back), so say in its instruction that it is in charge of that bug. It can start helper subagents of its own to split the work. You coordinate: reply to the user and pass on what the reports say.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

# Validity

## Invalid DateTimes

One of the most irritating aspects of programming with time is that it's possible to end up with invalid dates. This is a bit subtle: barring integer overflows, there's no count of milliseconds that don't correspond to a valid DateTime, but when working with calendar units, it's pretty easy to say something like "June 400th". Luxon considers that invalid and will mark it accordingly.

Unless you've asked Luxon to throw an exception when it creates an invalid DateTime (see more on that below), it will fail silently, creating an instance that doesn't know how to do anything. You can check validity with `isValid`:

```js
> var dt = DateTime.fromObject({ month: 6, day: 400 });
dt.isValid //=> false
```

All of the methods or getters that return primitives return degenerate ones:

```js
dt.year; //=>  NaN
dt.toString(); //=> 'Invalid DateTime'
dt.toObject(); //=> {}
```

Methods that return other Luxon objects will return invalid ones:

```js
dt.plus({ days: 4 }).isValid; //=> false
```

## Reasons a DateTimes can be invalid

The most common way to do that is to over- or underflow some unit:

- February 40th
- 28:00
- -4 pm
- etc

But there are other ways to do it:

```js
// specify a time zone that doesn't exist
DateTime.local().setZone("America/Blorp").isValid; //=> false

// provide contradictory information (here, this date is not a Wedensday)
DateTime.fromObject({ year: 2017, month: 5, day: 25, weekday: 3 }).isValid; //=> false
```

Note that some other kinds of mistakes throw, based on our judgment that they are more likely programmer errors than data issues:

```js
DateTime.local().set({ blorp: 7 }); //=> kerplosion
```

## Debugging invalid DateTimes

Because DateTimes fail silently, they can be a pain to debug. Luxon has some features that can help.

### invalidReason and invalidExplanation

Invalid DateTime objects are happy to tell you why they're invalid. `invalidReason` will give you a consistent error code you can use, whereas `invalidExplanation` will spell it out

```js
var dt = DateTime.local().setZone("America/Blorp");
dt.invalidReason; //=>  'unsupported zone'
dt.invalidExplantion; //=> 'the zone "America/Blorp" is not supported'
```

### throwOnInvalid

You can make Luxon throw whenever it creates an invalid DateTime. The message will combine `invalidReason` and `invalidExplanation`:

```js
Settings.throwOnInvalid = true;
DateTime.local().setZone("America/Blorp"); //=> Error: Invalid DateTime: unsupported zone: the zone "America/Blorp" is not supported
```

You can of course leave this on in production too, but be sure to try/catch it appropriately.

## Invalid Durations

Durations can be invalid too. The easiest way to get one is to diff an invalid DateTime.

```js
DateTime.local(2017, 28).diffNow().isValid; //=> false
```

## Invalid Intervals

Intervals can be invalid. This can happen a few different ways:

Summary of root cause:
`Interval.fromISO` unconditionally called `DateTime.fromISO(s, opts)` and `DateTime.fromISO(e, opts)` on both halves of the string. When one half is an ISO duration (valid `<start>/<duration>` or `<duration>/<end>` forms), `DateTime.fromISO` produces an invalid DateTime — and when `Settings.throwOnInvalid === true` it throws `InvalidDateTimeError` instead. Summary:
- Root cause: `objToLocalTS` in src/impl/util.js. For calendar years 0–99, `Date.UTC(year, ...)` maps to 19xx (1900+year). The old correction did `d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900)`, i.e. it first normalized the month/day overflow in the 19xx year and only then changed the year. Since the leap-year status of the 19xx year can differ from the target year (1900 is not a leap year but year 0 is; 2000 is a leap year but year 100 is not), the day-of-month got shifted by one when the date passed through February. E.g. `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ days: 61 })`: adjustTime builds {year: 99, month: 12, day: 92}; Date.UTC(99, 11, 92) normalizes to 2000-03-01 (2000 is leap, so Feb 29 exists); subtracting 1900 gives 0100-03-01, but year 100 has only 28 days in February, so the correct answer is 0100-03-02.
- Fix: set year, month and day together in the target year: `d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day);` so the out-of-range month/day are normalized using the target year's own leap rules.
- Diff: src/impl/util.js lines 166-171 (one line replaced, one comment added).

## Root cause

`objToLocalTS()` in `/luxon/src/impl/util.js` (the helper `DateTime#plus`/`#minus` reach via `adjustTime` → `objToLocalTS`). For calendar years 0–99, `Date.UTC(year, ...)` maps the year to 19xx, and the old correction was:

```js
d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900);
```

This first *normalizes* out-of-range month/day overflow inside the **19xx** year, and only then changes the year. Because the 19xx year's leap status can differ from the target year's (1900 is not leap but year 0 is; **2000 is leap but year 100 is not**), any date that passes through February gets shifted by one day.

Concrete failing case (the reported scenario): `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ days: 61 })`. `adjustTime` builds `{year: 99, month: 12, day: 92}`; `Date.UTC(99, 11, 92)` normalizes to `2000-03-01` (2000 is leap, so Feb 29 exists), then `-1900` yields `0100-03-01`. Year 100 has only 28 February days, so the correct answer is `0100-03-02`. (Pre-fix, the existing test `plus({ day: 2 })` passed by luck because 1999 and 99 are both non-leap.)

## Fix (minimal, only file changed: `/luxon/src/impl/util.js`, lines 166–171)

```diff
@@ -166,7 +166,8 @@ export function objToLocalTS(obj) {
   // for legacy reasons, years between 0 and 99 are interpreted as 19XX; revert that
   if (obj.year < 100 && obj.year >= 0) {
     d = new Date(d);
-    d.setUTCFullYear(d.getUTCFullYear() - 1900);
+    // set the month and day again, this is necessary because year 2000 is a leap year, but year 100 is not
+    d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day);
   }
   return +d;
 }
```

Setting year+month+day together makes the out-of-range month/day normalize using the **target** year's own leap rules. No other file touched; no test file modified.

# Support matrix

This page covers what platforms are supported by Luxon and what caveats apply to them.

## Official support

Luxon officially supports the last two versions of the major browsers, with some caveats. The table below shows which of the not-universally-supported features are available in what environments.

| Browser                          | Versions | Zones | Intl basics | Intl tokens | Intl relative time formatting |
| -------------------------------- | -------- | ----- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- |
| Chrome                           | >= 71    | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✓                             |
|                                  | >= 54    | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✗                             |
| Firefox                          | >= 65    | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✓                             |
| Edge                             | 18       | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 16       | ✓     | ✓           | ✗           | ✗                             |
| IE                               | 11       | ✗     | ✓           | ✗           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 10       | ✗     | ✗           | ✗           | ✗                             |
| Safari                           | 11       | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 10       | ✓     | ✗           | ✗           | ✗                             |
| iOS Safari (iOS version numbers) | >= 11    | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 10       | ✓     | ✗           | ✗           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 9        | ✗     | ✓           | ✗           | ✗                             |
| Node w/ICU                       | >= 8     | ✓     | ✓           | ✓           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 6        | ✗     | ✓           | ✗           | ✗                             |
| Node w/o ICU                     | >= 8     | ✓     | ✗           | ✗           | ✗                             |
|                                  | 6        | ✗     | ✗           | ✗           | ✗                             |

- Those capabilities are explained in the next sections, along with possible polyfill options
- "w/ICU" refers to providing Node with ICU data. See the [install](install.html#node) for instructions

## Internet Explorer and platform polyfills

If you're supporting IE 10 or 11, you need some polyfills just to make Luxon work at all.

With IE 11, you can just add a polyfill like this to get the JS features you need:

```html
<script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v2/polyfill.js?features=default,String.prototype.repeat,Array.prototype.find,Array.prototype.findIndex,Math.trunc,Math.sign"></script>
```

That hasn't checked off the other boxes in the chart above though, so keep reading for those.

With IE 10, you have the same problems as IE 11, except that you don't even get basic Intl support. You'll need to tack on the languages you wish to support. See the Basic Internationalization polyfill section below.

Alternatively, you can use a polyfilled build of Luxon, which you can find here:

- [Download full polyfilled build](../../global-filled/luxon.js)
- [Download minified polyfilled build](../../global-filled/luxon.min.js)

These use global polyfills, though, which means newer browsers will be running the injected code too. And the same doesn't-include-intl-and-zone-support caveats apply to it too.

## Effects of missing features

**If the platforms you're targeting has all its boxes above check off, ignore this section**.

In the support table above, you can see that some environments are missing capabilities. They affect a subset of Luxon's features that depend on specific APIs that some older browsers don't support.

1.  **Basic internationalization**. Luxon doesn't have internationalized strings in its code; instead it relies on the hosts implementation of the Intl API. This includes the very handy [toLocaleString](../class/src/datetime.js~DateTime.html#instance-method-toLocaleString). Most browsers and recent versions of Node support this.
2.  **Internationalized tokens**. Listing the months or weekdays of a locale and outputting or parsing ad-hoc formats in non-English locales requires that Luxon be able to programmatically introspect the results of an Intl call. It does this using Intl's [formatToParts](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/DateTimeFormat/formatToParts) method, which is a relatively recent addition in most browsers. So you could have the Intl API without having that.
3.  **Zones**. Luxon's support of IANA zones works by abusing the Intl API. That means you have to have that API and that the API must support a reasonable list of time zones. Zones are a recent addition to some platforms.

But how do those conversions actually work? First, uncontroversially:

 * 1 week = 7 days
 * 1 day = 24 hours
 * 1 hour = 60 minutes
 * 1 minute = 60 seconds
 * 1 second = 1000 milliseconds
 
These are always true and you can roll them up and down with consistency (e.g. `1 hour = 60 * 60 * 1000 milliseconds`). However, this isn't really true for the higher order units, which vary in length, even putting DSTs aside. A year is sometimes 365 days long and sometimes 366. Months are 28, 29, 30, or 31 days. By default Luxon converts between these units using what you might call "casual" conversions:

|         | Month | Week | Day |
| ---     | ---   |  --- | --- |
| Year    | 12    |   52 | 365 |
| Quarter | 3     |   13 |  91 |
| Month   |       |    4 |  30 |

These should match your intuition and for most purposes they work well. But they're not just wrong; they're not even self-consistent:

```js
dur.shiftTo('months').shiftTo('days').as('years') //=> 0.9863013698630136
```

This is because 12 * 30 != 365. These errors can be annoying, but they can also cause significant issues if the errors accumulate:

```js
var dur = Duration.fromObject({ years: 50000 });
DateTime.local().plus(dur.shiftTo('milliseconds')).year //=> 51984
DateTime.local().plus(dur).year                         //=> 52017
```

Those are 33 years apart! So Luxon offers an alternative conversion scheme called "longterm", based on the 400-year calendar cycle:

|         | Month |     Week |       Day |
|----     | ---   |      --- |       --- |
| Year    | 12    |  52.1775 |  365.2425 |
| Quarter |  3    | 13.04435 | 91.310625 |
| Month   |       | 4.348125 | 30.436875 |

You can see why these are irritating to work with, which is why they're not the default.

Luxon methods that create Durations de novo accept an option called `conversionAccuracy`. You can set it to "casual" or "longterm". It's a property of the Duration itself, so any conversions you do use the rule you've picked, and any new Durations you derive from it will retain that property.

```js
Duration.fromObject({ years: 23, conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
Duration.fromISO('PY23', { conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });

end.diff(start, 'days', { conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' })
```

## Root cause
`FixedOffsetZone.isValid` in `/luxon/src/zones/fixedOffsetZone.js` was hardcoded to `return true`, so a zone constructed with a non-numeric offset (`FixedOffsetZone.instance("blorp")`, `new FixedOffsetZone("blorp")`, `new FixedOffsetZone(undefined)`) reported `isValid === true` while its `fixed`/`offset()` were `NaN`. `DateTime`'s constructor (`src/datetime.js:385`) and the factories (`fromMillis`/`fromObject`/`setZone`, lines 531/618/1266) gate invalidity on `!zone.isValid`, so those DateTimes stayed "valid". `IANAZone` does the analogous thing via a stored `valid` flag (`isValidZone`), and `InvalidZone` returns `isValid === false`; `FixedOffsetZone` was the only zone that never checked its input.

```diff
-import { formatOffset, signedOffset } from "../impl/util.js";
+import { formatOffset, signedOffset, isNumber } from "../impl/util.js";
@@
   /** @override **/
   get isValid() {
-    return true;
+    return isNumber(this.fixed);
   }
```
(`isNumber` is the existing `typeof o === "number"` helper in `src/impl/util.js`; `NaN` is a number but is never passed as a fixed offset in practice — `zoneUtil.normalizeZone` only calls `FixedOffsetZone.instance` for `isNumber(input)` values, `IANAZone.parseGMTOffset` returns `parseInt` results, and `parseSpecifier` returns `signedOffset` results, so only non-numeric inputs are newly invalid. `isNumber` rather than `isInteger` was chosen to avoid rejecting any numeric offset.) `FixedOffsetZone.isValid` in `/luxon/src/zones/fixedOffsetZone.js` was hardcoded to `return true`, so a zone constructed with a non-numeric offset (`FixedOffsetZone.instance("blorp")`, `new FixedOffsetZone("blorp")`, `new FixedOffsetZone(undefined)`) reported `isValid === true` while its `fixed`/`offset()` were `NaN`. `DateTime`'s constructor (`src/datetime.js:385`) and the factories (`fromMillis`/`fromObject`/`setZone`, lines 531/618/1266) gate invalidity on `!zone.isValid`, so those DateTimes stayed "valid". `IANAZone` does the analogous thing via a stored `valid` flag (`isValidZone`), and `InvalidZone` returns `isValid === false`; `FixedOffsetZone` was the only zone that never checked its input.

## Fix (only file changed: `src/zones/fixedOffsetZone.js`)
```diff
-import { formatOffset, signedOffset } from "../impl/util.js";
+import { formatOffset, signedOffset, isNumber } from "../impl/util.js";
@@
   /** @override **/
   get isValid() {
-    return true;
+    return isNumber(this.fixed);
   }
```
(`isNumber` is the existing `typeof o === "number"` helper in `src/impl/util.js`; `NaN` is a number but is never passed as a fixed offset in practice — `zoneUtil.normalizeZone` only calls `FixedOffsetZone.instance` for `isNumber(input)` values, `IANAZone.parseGMTOffset` returns `parseInt` results, and `parseSpecifier` returns `signedOffset` results, so only non-numeric inputs are newly invalid. `isNumber` rather than `isInteger` was chosen to avoid rejecting any numeric offset.) ## Root cause

`src/duration.js` conversion matrices were **incomplete**: two entries were missing, so any conversion involving those pairs produced `NaN` (and `normalize()` returned `null` values, i.e. an invalid-looking duration).

- `casualMatrix.years` was missing `quarters: 4`
- `casualMatrix.quarters` was missing `seconds: 91 * 24 * 60 * 60`
- `accurateMatrix.years` was missing `quarters: 4`

The matrices are indexed `matrix[higherUnit][lowerUnit]` = how many lower units are in one higher unit, and both `convert()` (`matrix[toUnit][fromUnit]`) and `shiftTo()` (`matrix[higher][lower]`) rely on every ordered pair being present. The documented tables in `docs/math.md` (Year→Month 12 / Week 52 / Day 365; Quarter→Month 3 / Week 13 / Day 91) confirm the expected values.

Reproduced before the fix with a scratch script (`/tmp`, since deleted):
- `Duration.fromObject({years:1}).shiftTo("quarters").toObject()` → `{quarters: null}` (NaN)
- `Duration.fromObject({quarters:1}).shiftTo("seconds").toObject()` → `{seconds: null}` (NaN)
- `Duration.fromObject({years:1, quarters:1}).normalize().toObject()` → `{years: null, quarters: null}`
- `Duration.fromObject({quarters:1, seconds:1}).normalize().toObject()` → `{quarters: null, seconds: null}`
- longterm accuracy: `{years:1, quarters:1}` also NaN.

## Fix (only file changed: `/luxon/src/duration.js`, +3 lines)

```
@@ -30,6 +30,7 @@   casualMatrix = Object.assign({ years: {
+        quarters: 4,
@@ -44,6 +45,7 @@   quarters: {
+        seconds: 91 * 24 * 60 * 60,
@@ -62,6 +64,7 @@   accurateMatrix = Object.assign({ years: {
+        quarters: 4,
```

- `Duration.fromObject({[hi]:1}).shiftTo(lo).get(lo)` === documented matrix value: 36/36 ✓ (was NaN for years→quarters and quarters→seconds)
- reverse `{lo: matrixValue}.shiftTo(hi)` === 1: 36/36 ✓
- `as(lo)`: 36/36 ✓
- `normalize()` roll-up for every pair, positive and negative (`{hi:1, lo:c+1}` → `{hi:2, lo:1}`; `{hi:-1, lo:-(c+1)}` → `{hi:-2, lo:-1}`): 36/36 ✓
- `normalize()` over all 2-unit combinations with values 0/±1/±2/±3/12/28/30/32/0.5: 0 NaN, 0 non-finite, 0 empty results (previously NaN for years+quarters and quarters+seconds)
